What an agent is

Day 1 — the practical session

Matias Zaldarriaga

Ondas Gravitacionales e Investigación Asistida por IA

Use ← and →, or the dots at the top. p switches between reading size and presenting size.

Before I say anything

Open your terminal.

Start an agent and ask it to reproduce one of the two papers.

I am deliberately not telling you what to type.

The setup

Where to work, and things one could type

1. Get the papers.

cd <the course repo>
ls day1/papers/

  PhysRev.136.B1224.pdf   Peters 1964
  1608.01940v4.pdf        The basic physics of GW150914

2. Pick one.

Peters 1964 — analytic. Orbital decay of a binary from the quadrupole formula. Four pages, from 1964, and your agent may or may not have read it.

1608.01940 — observational. GW150914's masses from the strain data, with a ruler.

3. Make a working directory.

mkdir -p ~/gw-day1
cd ~/gw-day1
cp <repo>/day1/papers/*.pdf .

4. Start an agent, there.

claude
# or
codex

Work in an empty directory you own. The agent will read and write files in it. Never start one in your home directory or in a repository you care about.

Things one could type

Examples, not instructions. Type your own — the differences between what everyone asks for are the experiment.

Terse. “Reproduce this paper.”

Perfectly legitimate. Watch what it decides “reproduce” means.

Specific. “Read PhysRev.136.B1224.pdf. Derive equations (5.6) and (5.7) yourself and check them with sympy. Then reproduce Figure 1 exactly.”

Names the artefact, names the check — sympy is symbolic algebra in python: exact expressions, so “check” means an identity, not a float.

With a contract. “…and leave me: a script I can run, a figure, and a list of every claim you verified and how. Say explicitly which results you derived and which you recalled.”

The last sentence is the one that pays.

Also worth trying

  • Don't give it the PDF at all. Just name the paper. (What happens?)
  • Ask it to do the calculation before reading the paper, then compare.
  • Ask it what it is unsure about.

Set the dials before you start

Whatever you type, write down which model and which reasoning effort you used. Next stage. We need it for the comparison.

The two dials

The model, and how hard it thinks

Claude Code
claude                      # interactive
claude -p "…"               # headless, one shot

/model      →  Opus · Sonnet · Haiku
/effort     →  low … high … max

claude --dangerously-skip-permissions
Codex CLI
codex                       # interactive
codex exec "…"              # headless, one shot

/model      →  model + reasoning effort

codex --full-auto
codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox

Model. A bigger model is more expensive per token and usually better at holding a long argument together. It is not uniformly better.

Reasoning effort. How much thinking it does before acting. Costs time and tokens. For a derivation this matters more than the model.

These flags change every few months. claude --help, codex --help. Do not memorise them; memorise that the two dials exist, because everything else in this session depends on them.

The week, in one table

What a scientist actually does

The organising idea for the whole week. Not “can AI do science” — but which of these specific jobs can it hold, and what does it need in order to hold them?

The jobWhat it needs from a toolWhere it shows up this week
Read the literaturethe source, not a summary of ittoday — the paper is in the repo

Explore — try things, most of them wrongcheap iteration, no ceremonyevery workshop
Write codeyour conventions, your file layoutday 2
Run code you did not writedocs, source, the ability to read bothday 2 (gwpy, lal)
Run something heavya cluster, patience, a babysitterday 3
Make a figuredata provenance and a way to regenerate ittoday (marimo)
Keep track of what you learnednotes that survive the session endingtoday (the wiki)
Write the paperLaTeX, and everything above still reproducibleday 5
Give the talkslides that are built, not maintainedday 5

Every row is a place where the tool either fits your workflow or fights it. Most of the practical content of this course is about the fit.

While that runs

Three things worth understanding before you read the output

Your agent will take a while. Leave it. If it asks you something, answer briefly and let it continue.

the loop

Chat, agent, harness. A chatbot is text in, text out. An agent is the same model in a loop with tools. The harness is everything around it — and the part you configure.

context

It is one flat block of text, and it is finite. When it fills, it gets summarised, and you do not choose which detail is lost.

cold start

Close the terminal and it is gone. There is exactly one fix: write it down, in the project, in a form the agent will read next time.

All three in full, with the commands, are on using-the-tools.html — one page for the whole week, which fills in as the week goes. Read them while your run works.

Somebody else's run

Seeing gravitational waves, in four prompts

Mark Cheung, down the corridor at the Institute, wanted to see what a gravitational wave does at every viewing angle at once. He sent this over. We are going to sit in it.

What it is. One HTML file, 6.9 MB, no install and no network: the four prompts he typed, and beside each one the thing it produced. Five interactive visualisers of numerical-relativity waveforms, all embedded inside it.

What to watch for. The second prompt does not ask for a visualiser. It asks for eight candidate ways to draw the thing, side by side, so that he can choose. The third prompt is one sentence: “I like option 4.” Taste, in the loop, twice.

The two dials, from his work. All four prompts ran on the same model at the same reasoning effort — Opus, medium, unchanged between prompts — and his README says so. That is what the dials being recorded looks like.

day1/show/gw_tutorial.html, and his four prompts verbatim beside it in prompts.txt. Both are yours to keep — he wrote them to be reused for teaching. [src:borrowed — the file, the four prompts, the 6.9 MB and the model-and-effort line are Mark Ho-Yeuk Cheung's (IAS), handed over 2026-08-10 and reused with his permission; credit and licence in day1/show/CREDIT.md]

it opens on its own

It is not embedded here. It is self-contained, it is 6.9 MB, and it has its own navigation — open it in a second tab and come back to this one.

What I got

The algebra came back right. The figures made from data came back wrong.

I ran both papers before you did. One instruction, given twice: once to a four-page analytic paper, once to a paper whose first three figures are made from the strain itself.

Everything that could be checked against an equation was checked and passed. All three figures that touched data are wrong, each in a different way, and nothing in either repository noticed.

Two runs, and the lines they finished with

runmodeleffortformat asked fortokens in / outwallwhenreceipt
Peters 1964——tex → pdf, marimo → html, a script of assertions——2026-07-24run.log
11/11 reported results reproduced
GW150914, the basic physics——tex → pdf, marimo → html, a script of assertions, and three figures from strain——2026-07-24run.log
23/23 reported results reproduced
Fig 1 strain, Fig 2 spectrogram, Fig 3 chirp-mass ridge fit -> 36 Msun (paper 30-40)

Not recorded for these runs: tokens, wall time, model, reasoning effort. They predate the convention; the fields are here so a later run fills them.

That is the usual report: a date, a list of files, and a line saying it all worked. Both lines are true. Neither of them is about the three figures further down, because no assertion in either repository touches those figures at all.

what the record is, and what it is not

Both runs happened on 2026-07-24. The instructions on the next stages are the ones recorded in this repository — the standing rule the runs were given, and the wording this session has quoted since it was written. They are not a keystroke log, and no tokens, wall time, model or effort setting were recorded at the time.

That is a defect, not a style: from day 2 the prompts are kept verbatim as they are typed and the run records what it consumed. The empty columns above are what a run looks like when nobody wrote that down.

What was asked

Peters 1964 — section by section

Not “reproduce this paper”. The instruction names the unit of work (a section), what to produce for each one, and how each claim is to be checked.

Instruction 1 — as recorded

  


  
Four pages of analysis, from 1964, and no data anywhere in it.
    This is the easy case, and it is worth naming as the easy case before the hard one.







  
What came back

  
An argument you read, figures you can vary, assertions that fail loudly

one check I liked

      
Peters works a Sun-like binary with a 4.5-day period, gets a lifetime of about
        3×1012 years, and describes the separation as about ten solar
        radii. Both statements are his own text, in §V.
        [src:borrowed — the 4.5-day period and the "about ten solar
        radii" are Peters 1964 §V, p. B1228]

      
The lifetime comes back at 3e12 yr
        [src:solar_lifetime_yr]. The separation does not: Kepler at
        two solar masses and 4.5 days gives 14 R☉
        [src:solar_a_from_4p5d_Rsun], and ten solar radii would be
        a period of 2.6 d
        [src:solar_period_at_10Rsun_d]. The lifetime is right; the
        separation in the text is rounded.

      
Unimportant to the physics, and completely
        characteristic. It is the difference between a reproduction and a paraphrase, and
        neither I nor an agent would have noticed it without running the number.

    

  







  
What was asked

  
GW150914 — the same instruction, on a paper with data in it


  
The one change: this paper's first three figures are made from the strain,
    not from the algebra. So the run had to fetch data and use a package neither of us had
    used before.


  

    
 Instruction 2 — as recorded

    

  


  
It fetched 32 s of H1 and L1 strain around the event from GWOSC at
    4096 Hz and cached it to a local array, so the analysis needs no network, and it used
    gwpy in a separate environment — the day-1 environment deliberately
    has no gravitational-wave stack in it.

the check I care about most

      
That peak luminosity equals −dE/dt from Peters'
        circular da/dt, computed from the other paper and agreeing to
        zero relative error
        [src:peak_luminosity_vs_peters_relerr]. Two papers, fifty
        years apart, are the same formula read from opposite ends. An independent route
        agreeing is worth more than any number of internal assertions.

    

  







  
What came back, second half

  
The three figures made from strain


  

    
Fig. 1 — the band-passed strain

      

    
Fig. 2 — the spectrogram

      

    
Fig. 3 — the frequency track and its fit

      

  


  

    
Every one of them is wrong, in a different way. The next four stages are
      the four failures, one at a time, each beside the paper's own figure.


    
Two of the three were caught by someone
      who has seen enough of these plots to know what one looks like. The third was caught
      by nobody, and the fourth failure is about why.

  







  
Failure 1

  
The missing step, and a sign


  

    
The paper's Fig. 1

      

    
What we produced

      

    
The same code, two lines changed

      

  


  

    

      

        
Cause 1 — the pass band is not flat.

        
The code did what the paper's text says: band-pass
          35–350 Hz, notch, no whitening. But inside that band the noise still varies
          by a factor of a few hundred, peaking at 37 Hz — so a plain
          band-pass leaves the low edge of the band dominant. That is the big slow wobble.
          The paper never mentions whitening (day 2's subject). It clearly whitened.

      

      

        
Cause 2 — the shift went the wrong way.

        
The paper shifts H1 back by 6.9 ms. The
          code added it, putting the two chirps 14 ms apart instead of on top of each other.
          Cross-correlating the whitened streams recovers −7.3 ms on its own —
          the data will tell you the answer if you ask it.

      

    


    
What caught it: someone who has seen enough of these
      plots to know what one looks like. No assertion in the repository would ever
      have fired.
      [src:borrowed — the 6.9 ms shift and the band and notch
      prescription are the paper's own (1608.01940 §Fig 1); the cross-correlation recovery
      and the noise variation across the band are the session artefact's own
      measurements]

  







  
Failure 2

  
Energy where the label says amplitude


  

    
The paper's Fig. 2 — colour bar 0–8, “normalized amplitude”

      

    
Ours — colour bar 0–25, “normalized energy”

      

  


  

    

      

        
What it did. A gwpy
          Q-transform, plotted raw. That function returns normalised
          energy; the paper's colour bar is normalised
          amplitude — the square root.

      

      

        
Why it is wrong. Two different
          quantities under the same axis label. The colour ceiling was then hand-set to 25
          — vmax=25 in the plotting call — until the picture looked
          right, rather than matched to the paper's. The transform's own Q range was picked
          by hand too, and differs from the one used for Fig. 3, with no reason recorded for
          either.

      

      

        
What caught it. Matias, by
          eye — “your signal looks much brighter.” The chirp is
          visible in both, which is exactly why nobody looked twice.

      

    


    
Fixable in one line — take the
      square root and set the limit to the paper's — and that is the point. It was
      never wrong in a way that broke anything; it was wrong in a way that no test could
      see, and only a comparison against the original catches it.

  







  
Failure 3

  
It did not do what it said


  

    
The paper's Fig. 3 — nine points, with error bars

      

    
Ours — a dense, stepped ridge

      

  


  

    

      

        
What the paper says to do. Measure the
          time between successive zero crossings of the band-passed strain,
          take f = 1/(2Δt), average five adjacent crossings where the signal is weak,
          combine H1 and L1.

      

      

        
What it actually did. Took the peak of
          each column of the Q-transform. The steps are the transform's frequency bins. This
          is a different measurement of a different thing — and the file's own
          docstring says “from zero-crossings”.

      

      

        
What caught it.
          Nothing. The fitted chirp mass landed inside the range the paper
          states — the line quoted in the run table above — so the number agreed
          while the method did not.

      

    


    
The best of the three. The docstring
      describes the paper's method; the code below it does something else; the answer still
      came out in range. A right answer obtained the wrong way is the hardest failure to
      catch, because the only thing you normally check is the answer.

  







  
Failure 4

  
Twenty-three out of twenty-three


  
The run log for that exercise says the reproduction is complete and every assertion
    passes. It does. And not one of those assertions touches any of the three figures you
    just saw.


  

    
check("(Fig 3)  f^-8/3 straight-line fit recovers M = 30 Msun",
      abs(Mfit - 30) < 1e-6)

  


  
Read the tolerance. No measurement of real data recovers
    30.000000
    [src:fig3_method_recovers_mc_msun]. That check generates a
    frequency track from a known chirp mass and fits it back — it
    tests the algebra of the fitting routine, and nothing else. But it is named after
    Figure 3, and it sits in a list that prints a green total.


  
So the honest state of that exercise: the analytic half is verified; the data
    half was never checked at all — and the receipt does not say so.







  
The pattern

  
They cluster


  
Across all of them, the failures are not random. They cluster:


  

    
Failure modeWhat it looks likeWhat defends against it

    
Recall dressed as derivationthe right final answer, with a derivation that does not produce itask which steps were derived and which recalled

    
Confident interpolationa plausible coefficient where the real one is unusualcheck against a printed number

    
Silent unit errorseverything consistent, one constant in the wrong systemdimensional analysis; a second implementation

    
Claiming without running“the fit converges” — no log, no outputask for the receipt, always

    
Drifting under a full contextfine early, degraded late, no announcementbound the task; start fresh

    
Agreeing with youyou suggest something wrong and it goes alongask it to argue against you

    
Uncovered by constructiona green summary line over work that no assertion touchesmake it state what it did not check

  


  

    
None of these are fixed by a better model. They are fixed by checks.


    
Questions of that kind, grouped by what
      each one is for, are in self-check.html. Example questions, not a form:
      the point is to invent the ones your own run needs.

  







  
Before the next session

  
What to do with the rest of the week


  

    

      
Physics

      
    
        
  • What separation must two 30 M☉ black holes have to merge within a Hubble
          time?
    • 
        
  • How does eccentricity change that?
    • 
        
  • Run the whole chain again on a second event — GW230814,
          in the repo.
    • 
      

    

    

      
Ask for more than an answer

      
Make it explain the same result at three levels. Make it
        visualise something you only have as algebra. Make it
        derive a result a second way and reconcile the two.

      
Then push on the boundaries:
        where does each approximation break, and what happens on the other side?

    

    

      
The controlled experiment

      
Take one task and run it several ways: two models, two effort
        settings, terse prompt vs contract prompt. Ask the same questions of each. Report
        what actually moved the answer.

      
One sample per cell — report what
        you saw, not what is true in general.

    

  


  

    
Come back with a vault containing pages neither of us wrote by hand
      — and at least one page where you corrected something the agent got wrong.


    
Every exercise the course sets is on one page,
      homework.html. Every concept this week introduces, and the day it
      arrives: using-the-tools.html. Pick what interests you; nobody is
      expected to do all of it.


    
To take away

    
    
      
  • The loop is the difference. A chatbot guesses about your files;
        an agent reads them, runs things, and can be asked for the receipt.
    • 
      
  • Context is finite and cold starts are real. Everything you want
        to survive must be written to disk in a form that gets read next time.
    • 
      
  • Formats decide whether you can review the output — and
        review, not generation, is the bottleneck.
    • 
      
  • You cannot tell a good derivation from a bad one by reading it.
        Ask for checks, not answers.
    • 
      
  • The harness is the part you control, and that is where the
        leverage is.
    • 
    


    
None of this is settled. It is what
      one person does in July 2026, and half of it will look naive in a year. Take it as a
      starting point and go argue with it.
